title: Wealth, rule and wisdom in the teaching of Jesus
source_text: Σαφῆ μὲν οὖν καὶ ἐκ τούτων, πῶς Ἰησοῦς ὁ „Ναζωραῖος“ ἄνθρωπος οὐκ ἀντινομοθετεῖ τοῖς περὶ πλούτου καὶ τῶν ἐξισταμένων εἰρημένοις περὶ τοῦ δύσκολον εἶναι πλούσιον εἰσέρχεσθαι εἰς τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ βασιλείαν· εἴτε πλούσιόν τις λαμβάνει ἁπλούστερον τὸν ὑπὸ πλούτου περισπώμενον καὶ ὡς ὑπὸ ἀκάνθης αὐτοῦ ἐμποδιζόμενον φέρειν τοὺς τοῦ λόγου καρποὺς εἴτε καὶ τὸν ἐν τοῖς ψευδέσι δόγμασι πλουτοῦντα, περὶ οὗ ἐν Παροιμίαις γέγραπται· „κρείσσων πτωχὸς δίκαιος ἢ πλούσιος ψεύστης.“ εἰκὸς δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ „ὁ θέλων ἐν ὑμῖν εἶναι πρῶτος ἔστω πάντων διάκονος“ καὶ „οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν κατακυριεύουσιν αὐτῶν“ καὶ „οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες ἐν αὐτοῖς εὐεργέται καλοῦνται“ εἰληφέναι τὸν Κέλσον ὅτι Ἰησοῦς φιλαρχίαν ἐκώλυεν, ἥντινα οὐκ ἐναντίαν εἶναι νομιστέον τοῦ „ἄρξεις σὺ ἐθνῶν πολλῶν, σοῦ δὲ οὐκ ἄρξουσι,“ μάλιστα διὰ τὰ ἀποδεδομένα εἰς τὴν λέξιν. ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις παραῤῥίπτει περὶ τῆς σοφίας ὁ Κέλσος, οἰόμενος τὸν Ἰησοῦν διδάσκειν μὴ παριτητὸν εἶναι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα τῷ σοφῷ. εἴπωμεν δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· ποίῳ σοφῷ; εἰ μὲν γὰρ τούτῳ, ὃς πεποίωται κατὰ τὴν λεγομένην σοφίαν „τοῦ κόσμου τούτου,“ ουσαν μωρίαν „παρὰ τῷ θεῷ.“ καὶ ἡμεῖς φήσομεν μὴ παριτητὸν εἶναι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα τῷ οὕτως σοφῷ· εἰ δὲ σοφίαν τις νοήσαι τὸν Χριστὸν, ἐπεὶ Χριστός ἐστι θεοῦ δύναμις καὶ θεοῦ σοφία, οὐ μόνον παριτητὸν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα τῷ οὕτως σοφῷ λέγομεν εἶναι, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλῷ τῶν μὴ τοιούτων διαφέρειν τὸν κεκοσμημένον χαρίσματί φαμεν λόγῳ „σοφίας“ καλουμένῳ, διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος διδομένῳ.
pass_a_gloss: Clear (σαφής) then also from these things, how Jesus the 'Nazarene' (Ναζωραῖος) man does not legislate-against (ἀντινομοθετέω) by the things said (εἰρημένα) about wealth (πλοῦτος) and about those being astonished / standing aside (ἐξίσταμαι), concerning its being hard (δύσκολος) for a rich man (πλούσιος) to enter into the kingdom (βασιλεία) of God; whether one takes (λαμβάνω) 'rich' more simply (ἁπλούστερον) as the one distracted (περισπάω) by wealth and as by thorn (ἄκανθα) hindered (ἐμποδίζω) by it from bearing (φέρω) the fruits (καρπός) of the word (λόγος), or also the one being rich (πλουτέω) in false doctrines (ψευδῆ δόγματα), about whom in Proverbs it is written: 'better (κρείσσων) a poor man (πτωχός) righteous (δίκαιος) than a rich man liar (ψεύστης).' Likely (εἰκός) from 'the one wishing among you to be first, let him be servant (διάκονος) of all' and 'the rulers (ἄρχοντες) of the nations (ἔθνη) lord it over (κατακυριεύω) them' and 'those exercising authority (ἐξουσιάζω) among them are called benefactors (εὐεργέται)' Celsus has taken (λαμβάνω, perf.) that Jesus forbade (κωλύω) love of rule (φιλαρχία), which one must not think (νομιστέον) contrary (ἐναντίος) to 'you shall rule (ἄρχω) over many nations, but they shall not rule over you,' especially because of the things rendered (ἀποδίδωμι, i.e. explanations given) for the passage (λέξις). Next after these Celsus throws in alongside (παραρρίπτω) about wisdom (σοφία), thinking Jesus teaches it not to be accessible (παριτητός) to the Father for the wise man (σοφός). Let us say to him: to what sort of wise man? If to this one, who has been qualified/shaped (ποιόω) according to the so-called wisdom 'of this world (κόσμος),' being foolishness (μωρία) 'with God,' we too shall say there is no access to the Father for the one so wise; but if one should understand (νοέω) Christ as wisdom, since Christ is power (δύναμις) of God and wisdom of God, we say not only that there is access to the Father for one so wise, but also we say that the one adorned (κοσμέω) with the gift (χάρισμα) called word (λόγος) of 'wisdom,' given (δίδωμι) through the Spirit (πνεῦμα), differs much from (surpasses, διαφέρω) those not such.
pass_b_english: From these points too, then, it is clear how Jesus, the “Nazarene” man, does not lay down contrary laws in what he said about wealth and about those who were amazed, namely, that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:23–26; Luke 18:24). This holds whether one takes the “rich man” more simply as the one who is distracted by wealth and hindered by it, as by thorns, from bearing the fruits of the word (Matthew 13:22), or as the one who is rich in false doctrines, of whom it is written in Proverbs: “Better a poor man who is righteous than a rich man who is a liar” (Proverbs 19:22).

It is likely that Celsus took the idea that Jesus forbade the love of rule from the sayings “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the servant of all” (Mark 10:43–44; compare Mark 9:35), “The rulers of the nations lord it over them” (Matthew 20:25), and “Those who exercise authority among them are called benefactors” (Luke 22:25). This must not be thought contrary to “You shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you” (Deuteronomy 15:6), especially in view of the explanations already given of that text.

Next after these points Celsus throws in something about wisdom, supposing that Jesus teaches that the wise man has no access to the Father. Let us say to him: Which wise man? If he means the one who has been shaped by what is called the wisdom “of this world,” which is foolishness “with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19), we too shall say that the man who is wise in this way has no access to the Father. But if one understands Wisdom to be Christ, since Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), we say not only that the man who is wise in this way has access to the Father; we also say that the one adorned with the gift called the word of “wisdom,” which is given through the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:8), far surpasses those who are not such.

choices.choice: Origen answers the list of charges Celsus made in 7.18 (wealth, love of rule, wisdom, glory). The opening clause τοῖς περὶ πλούτου καὶ τῶν ἐξισταμένων εἰρημένοις is awkward as printed. It is read as ‘what he said about wealth and about those who were amazed’ (keeping both περί phrases; the scene of the disciples’ amazement at Mark 10:24, 26; compare Matthew 19:25 ἐξεπλήσσοντο); ἐξίσταμαι could also mean ‘those who give up (their wealth)’, but the following περὶ τοῦ δύσκολον εἶναι clause fits the Gospel scene. The object of ἀντινομοθετεῖ is not stated; it echoes Celsus’s verb in 7.18 (‘lays down contrary laws’), so no ‘to Moses’ is added. ‘Nazarene’ is in quotation marks because Origen is repeating Celsus’s phrase ὁ Ναζωραῖος ἄνθρωπος. Proverbs 19:22: the Septuagint reads κρεῖσσον δὲ πτωχὸς δίκαιος ἢ πλούσιος ψεύστης (compare Proverbs 28:6). The first-servant saying blends Mark 10:43–44 (πρῶτος ... πάντων δοῦλος) with Mark 9:35 (πάντων διάκονος); compare Matthew 20:26–27. Luke 22:25 reads οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες αὐτῶν; Origen has ἐν αὐτοῖς. ἥντινα grammatically refers to φιλαρχίαν; the sense is that Jesus’ ban on love of rule is not contrary to Deuteronomy 15:6, so it is rendered ‘This’. ‘The explanations already given’ (τὰ ἀποδεδομένα εἰς τὴν λέξιν) points back to Origen’s reading of Deuteronomy 15:6 as rule by the word in 7.19 and 7.21. παριτητός (‘accessible, to be approached’) is Celsus’s word from 7.18. ‘Wisdom’ is capitalised where it names Christ.

Opening clause: 'his sayings about wealth, and in his words to those who were astonished' changed to 'what he said about wealth and about those who were amazed, namely,' so both περί phrases are kept (the earlier 'to those' changed the preposition); note updated
Checked Proverbs 19:22 LXX, Mark 10:43-44 / 9:35, Matthew 20:25, Luke 22:25, Deuteronomy 15:6, 1 Corinthians 3:19, 1:24, 12:8 against the Greek: all correct

choices.choice: 7.23: what τῶν ἐξισταμένων means is still uncertain. It could be 'those who were amazed' (the disciples, Mark 10:24-26) or 'those who give up their possessions'. The text keeps the first reading, and the translator note gives both. Owner may wish to confirm.
